extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating actual/constructive reduction to practice, reasonable diligence, and obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 for patent examination and interference contexts. Covers testing, recognition, inurement, accounting for diligence, and application of KSR/Graham principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual reduction to practice — testing sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: For an actual reduction to practice, the invention must have been sufficiently tested to demonstrate that it will work for its intended purpose, but it need not be in a commercially satisfactory stage of development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The character of testing necessary varies with the complexity of the invention and the problem it solved; for very simple devices construction alone may suffice to demonstrate workability (e.g., King Instrument Corp. v. Otari Corp.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing required to establish actual reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature of testing required depends on the particular facts of each case; tests may be sufficient where less than all conditions of actual use are duplicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If tests do not duplicate each and every condition of actual use, the evidence must establish a relationship between the subject matter, the test condition and the intended functional setting of the invention; bench or laboratory conditions are acceptable if they adequately relate to real use (citations: Gellert v. Wanberg; Wells v. Fremont).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition/appreciation requirement for reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduction to practice requires contemporaneous recognition and appreciation of the invention by the inventor; subsequent testing or later recognition may not be used to establish that contemporaneous appreciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An experiment only constitutes an actual reduction to practice if there was contemporaneous appreciation of the invention (Cooper v. Goldfarb); an inventor need not fully understand why it works, but must appreciate the invention when the reduction to practice occurred (Parker v. Frilette).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inurement by non-inventor — three-prong test
rubrics_metrics.description: Before a non-inventor’s recognition can inure to the inventor’s benefit, three conditions must be met: (1) the inventor conceived of the invention, (2) the inventor had an expectation that the embodiment tested would work for the intended purpose, and (3) the inventor submitted the embodiment for testing for that intended purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any prong is missing (e.g., samples sent but inventor unaware of the relevant property or did not submit for the intended test), the non-inventor’s recognition does not inure (Genentech v. Chiron; Cooper v. Goldfarb examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete limitation reduction in interference proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: In an interference, the device reduced to practice must include every limitation of the count; every limitation is material and must be proved to establish actual reduction to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no doctrine of equivalents in an interference context — remedy is to amend the count to conform to the proofs (Fredkin v. Irasek; Meitzner v. Corte; Hull v. Bonis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Known utility at time of reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention is not actually reduced to practice unless there is a known/practical utility at the time of reduction to practice (except for plant and design inventions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility must be demonstrated by testing or other accepted evidence; for compounds, animal tests that reasonably correlate to human utility may suffice; a demonstrated substantial utility for any purpose (when no specific utility recited) can be sufficient (Wiesner v. Weigert; Ciric v. Flanigen; Rey-Bellet v. Engelhardt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Probable utility may be insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A probable utility does not establish practical utility required to prove reduction to practice; strong probability or indication is insufficient without testing or ability to 'foretell with certainty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screening tests indicating possible utility are insufficient; evidence must be judged as a whole and reasonable correlation between observed properties and suggested uses can sometimes be sufficient (Bindra v. Kelly; Wu v. Jucker; Nelson v. Bowler caveat).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of reasonable diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Diligence under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) encompasses both 'attorney-diligence' and 'engineering-diligence' and does not require that an inventor or attorney abandon all other work to focus solely on the particular invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable diligence means reasonably continuous effort, not constant daily activity; attorneys with reasonable backlogs or parallel work may still be diligent if work is conducted expeditiously (Keizer v. Bradley; Emery v. Ronden; Bey v. Kollonitsch; Perfect Surgical Techniques discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical period for establishing diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: For a first conceiver but later reducer, the critical period for diligence begins just prior to the entry in the field by the party who was first to reduce to practice and continues until the first conceiver reduces to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What constitutes 'entry into the field' depends on what the first reducer relies upon (e.g., conception plus diligence, actual reduction to practice, constructive reduction by filing, or priority under 35 U.S.C. 119); see cited cases for different fact patterns (Hull v. Davenport; Rebstock v. Flouret; Justus v. Appenzeller).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for entire diligence period
rubrics_metrics.description: The entire period during which diligence is required must be accounted for by either affirmative acts or acceptable excuses; reasonable continuity is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely stating diligence is insufficient; even short gaps (e.g., 2 days in some circumstances) can be fatal absent evidence; acceptable excuses are limited (vacation, illness may be considered; lack of funding or personnel generally not acceptable); weigh the body of evidence to determine whether the invention was not abandoned or unreasonably delayed (Gould v. Schawlow; In re Mulder; Perfect Surgical Techniques discussion and case citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct relation of relied-upon work to reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Work relied upon to show reasonable diligence must be directly related to the reduction to practice of the invention in issue; work on related subject matter is insufficient unless it is closely related and directed to attaining reduction to practice of the claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have allowed reliance on work for closely related inventions when part of the same inventive endeavor (e.g., grandparent applications), but fortuitous results achieved while working on a different invention do not demonstrate diligence toward the invention in issue (Naber v. Cricchi; Scott v. Koyama; Gunn v. Bosch; Ginos v. Nedelec).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence in preparing and filing patent application
rubrics_metrics.description: Diligence of the attorney in preparing and filing the patent application inures to the benefit of the inventor; conception can be established when a draft of the application was finished by the attorney on behalf of the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attorney need only exercise reasonable diligence; short delays (e.g., six days to execute and file) may be acceptable; work on related cases that substantially contributed can be credited as diligence (Haskell v. Coleburne; Bey v. Kollonitsch; Perfect Surgical Techniques quote on preparation).

rubrics_metrics.name: End of diligence period — actual or constructive reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of the diligence period is marked by either an actual reduction to practice or a constructive reduction to practice (e.g., filing an application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is immaterial that the end is fixed by a constructive rather than actual reduction to practice — constructive R2P can end the diligence period (Justus v. Appenzeller).

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR principles for obviousness — flexible approach
rubrics_metrics.description: KSR v. Teleflex reaffirmed a more flexible approach to obviousness, rejecting an overly rigid application of the teaching-suggestion-motivation (TSM) test and endorsing use of common sense and broader reasoning when supported by a reasoned explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should consider that combination of familiar elements yielding predictable results is likely obvious; courts and examiners need not limit themselves to references solving the exact same problem; invoking common sense to supply missing limitations requires evidence and a searching, reasoned basis (KSR summary and Arendi v. Apple discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiries for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness analysis follows Graham v. John Deere: (A) determine scope and content of the prior art; (B) ascertain differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; (C) resolve the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary considerations (objective evidence) should be evaluated where present; the Graham factors remain the controlling inquiries and may be reordered as appropriate in particular cases (Graham factors reiterated and applied in KSR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective evidence (secondary considerations) in obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence relevant to obviousness (sometimes called 'secondary considerations') may include commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, and unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such evidence may be included in the specification on filing or provided timely during prosecution; the weight given is case-by-case and presentation of evidence does not make it dispositive — it must be considered as part of the overall Graham analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for examiners to articulate findings and rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel act as factfinders and must ensure the written record includes findings of fact concerning the state of the art and the teachings of applied references when making an obviousness rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must provide explanation(s) to support an obviousness rejection so the applicant can respond; factual findings and rationale should include how a person of ordinary skill would have understood prior art teachings and why combination or modification is supported (35 U.S.C. 132 requirement; guidance to 'clearly set forth findings of fact and the rationale(s)').
